analysis.one_liner: Exempts health insurers from penalties for selling plans that violate most Affordable Care Act rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and to a health subcommittee weeks later, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the federal government from fining or punishing health insurers and employers who offer health plans that break most Affordable Care Act rules. Only two protections would stay enforceable: insurers could not deny coverage for preexisting conditions, and children could remain on a parent's plan until age 26. Every other ACA requirement — like mandated benefits, limits on out-of-pocket costs, and rules on how premiums must be spent — could be violated with no penalty. The bill never advanced past a committee referral and died at the end of the congressional session.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers and the employers who sponsor group health plans would gain: they could sell or offer plans that skip Affordable Care Act requirements — such as covering essential health benefits, capping out-of-pocket costs, or spending a set share of premiums on actual medical care — without facing any federal fine. Policyholders and the public would gain only the two preserved protections, and lose the rest of the ACA's enforceable standards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: It would bar any federal agency from fining or otherwise penalizing a health insurer or group health plan sponsor for failing to comply with any applicable Affordable Care Act requirement.
It preserves only two requirements: the ban on excluding preexisting conditions and the rule allowing children to stay on a parent's plan until age 26.
It applies to every kind of insurance seller — sole proprietors, partnerships, for-profit and nonprofit corporations — not just a narrow slice of the market.

analysis.who_pays: People with health coverage would bear the cost if the bill passed: insurers could strip benefits, raise charges, or sell thin plans that meet none of the ACA's standards except the preexisting-condition and age-26 rules, and no federal agency could penalize them for it. The preexisting-condition guarantee itself would be harder to rely on, since a promise to cover everyone means little if the plans are allowed to be unaffordable or cover almost nothing.

drawbacks.text: The bill would nullify enforcement of most Affordable Care Act coverage standards, including requirements for essential health benefits, limits on out-of-pocket costs, and rules on how much of premium revenue insurers must spend on medical care, leaving only the preexisting-condition and dependent-age protections intact.

A prohibition on refusing preexisting conditions is hard to enforce if an insurer can otherwise design plans to be unaffordable or to cover very little; the bill leaves the guarantee standing while removing penalties for every other rule that makes coverage meaningful.

Insurers and plan sponsors that keep complying with the ACA would face a cost disadvantage against competitors freed to sell skimpier coverage, potentially pulling the market toward low-benefit plans even for people who want comprehensive options.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would hand insurers and large employers a sweeping exemption from federal health insurance rules while keeping only two protections in place. Even the two kept protections would be weaker in practice, since much of the anti-discrimination and dependent-coverage framework depends on the same rules the bill would nullify. The benefit to the public is unclear at best; the cost — weaker coverage standards with no penalty for cutting benefits or raising charges — is concrete. The bill died without a hearing or vote, and given its scope and narrow sponsorship that was the likely outcome regardless.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its health subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 352 was introduced in the House on January 8, 2019 and referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
On January 25, 2019 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, the last action of record.
No further action was taken through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, so the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary policyholders are better off, because the Affordable Care Act's coverage standards — required benefits, out-of-pocket limits, and other consumer rules — remain fully enforceable with penalties intact. Insurers and plan sponsors did not get the exemption they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and the ACA's coverage standards

for.name: Rep. Ted Yoho
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt health insurers and group health plan sponsors from penalties for violating Affordable Care Act requirements.

for.name: 4 of 197 House Republicans
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Weber of Texas, Babin, DesJarlais, Gibbs)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other members added their names during the session.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled, so the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had an all-Republican, five-member sponsorship and died in a committee controlled by Democrats without any recorded vote, so the contest never reached the floor.

industries.note: The bill would free insurers from federal fines for selling plans that fail most Affordable Care Act standards, such as required benefits and limits on out-of-pocket costs, while keeping only the preexisting-condition and dependent-age rules. If passed, insurers could charge more for less coverage without penalty; because the bill died, current law still applies.

Employers who run group health plans would be equally exempt from penalties for non-compliant plans, gaining flexibility to offer thinner coverage. The bill's failure leaves their compliance obligations unchanged.
